hints: Focus on the amount of product formed, think what quantity in moles makes this definition standard and comparable for all compounds.
Focus on the starting materials, think what pure substances a compound must be made directly from for a formation enthalpy.
walkthrough:
Pin down the amount formed**
Think of formation as a recipe for making a substance. By definition you always make exactly $1$ mole of the compound, no more, no less. So you say: the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed. That one mole part is essential for the first mark.

Pin down what you start from**
Now picture what you start with. You do not start from other compounds, you start from the elements that make up the compound, each in its normal, most stable form at $298\text{ K}$ and $101\text{ kPa}$. For example, carbon as $\text{C(s)}$, oxygen as $\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}$, iron as $\text{Fe(s)}$. That gives you: from its elements in their standard states.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions.

hints: Remember the rule from (a), each equation must make exactly one mole of product only, using the elements $\text{Fe(s)}$, $\text{C(s)}$ and $\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}$ as reactants.

Look at the completed $\text{CO}_{2}$ example $\text{C(s)} + \text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_{2}\text{(g)}$, then balance $\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ and $\text{CO}$ to give one mole of product, using fractions of $\text{O}_{2}$ if needed.
walkthrough:
Apply the one mole rule**
Keep your definition in mind. A formation equation must produce $1$ mole of the named product. So for iron(III) oxide the product must be $1\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3}\text{(s)}$, and for carbon monoxide the product must be $1\text{CO(g)}$. The reactants can only be the elements in their standard states: $\text{Fe(s)}$, $\text{C(s)}$ and $\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}$.

Write and balance each equation**
For $\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ you need $2$ irons and $3$ oxygens on the left, so: $$2\text{Fe(s)} + \frac{3}{2}\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3}\text{(s)}$$ Fractions are allowed here because you must keep the product as one mole. For $\text{CO}$ you need $1$ carbon and $1$ oxygen atom, so: $$\text{C(s)} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CO(g)}$$ Include all state symbols, as they show standard states.

hints: Recall the Hess cycle result for formation data, enthalpy of reaction equals sum of formation enthalpies of products minus sum of formation enthalpies of reactants.

Check the balancing numbers in reaction 2, $\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3} + 3\text{CO} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe} + 3\text{CO}_{2}$, and remember that elements such as $\text{Fe}$ have zero enthalpy of formation.
walkthrough:
Set up the Hess law expression**
Imagine breaking reactants down to elements then rebuilding products. That shortcut gives you products minus reactants. For reaction 2: $$\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3} + 3\text{CO} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe} + 3\text{CO}_{2}$$ So: $$\Delta H_{\text{r}} = [2\Delta H_{\text{f}}^{\ominus}(\text{Fe}) + 3\Delta H_{\text{f}}^{\ominus}(\text{CO}_{2})] - [\Delta H_{\text{f}}^{\ominus}(\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3}) + 3\Delta H_{\text{f}}^{\ominus}(\text{CO})]$$ Since $\text{Fe}$ is an element in its standard state, $\Delta H_{\text{f}}^{\ominus}(\text{Fe}) = 0$.

Substitute values and calculate**
Put in the Table 4.1 values $\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3} = -824.2$, $\text{CO} = -110.5$, $\text{CO}_{2} = -393.5$, all in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$: $$\Delta H_{\text{r}} = [3 \times (-393.5)] - [(-824.2) + 3 \times (-110.5)]$$ $$\Delta H_{\text{r}} = (-1180.5) - (-1155.7) = -24.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows the reaction is slightly exothermic.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{\text{r}} = \Sigma \Delta H_{\text{f}}^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_{\text{f}}^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$
$= [3 \times (-393.5)] - [(-824.2) + 3 \times (-110.5)] = -24.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
